questions.q: What is the single most important difference between a Service Control Policy (SCP) and an IAM policy?
options: An SCP can grant permissions directly to a user, while an IAM policy cannot
An SCP sets the maximum permissions available to accounts in scope and can only restrict, never grant, while IAM policies are what actually grant access
SCPs and IAM policies are evaluated by completely unrelated services with no interaction
SCPs only apply to the management account, never to member accounts
questions.explain: An SCP defines a ceiling on what's possible in accounts it covers — it can deny, but it can never be the reason a request succeeds. The actual grant always has to come from an IAM policy inside the account.

questions.q: In AWS Organizations, what does attaching a policy to an Organizational Unit (OU) do?
options: It only affects the management account, regardless of which accounts are in the OU
It applies the policy to every account nested underneath that OU
It converts every account in the OU into a new management account
It has no effect unless each member account separately opts in
questions.explain: OUs are groupings of accounts, and a policy attached at the OU level applies to every account underneath it — letting you set a guardrail once instead of repeating it account by account.

questions.q: In the region-restriction SCP example that uses NotAction with iam:*, organizations:*, sts:*, and support:*, why are those services excluded from the deny?
options: Because those services are too insecure to restrict with an SCP
Because NotAction only works with Allow statements, never Deny
Because those are global services that don't operate within a single region, so excluding them keeps the account's core management APIs from breaking
Because SCPs cannot reference IAM actions under any circumstance
questions.explain: IAM, Organizations, STS, and Support are global services with no regional concept. Excluding them from a region-restricting Deny keeps the account manageable instead of locking out account administration entirely.

questions.q: An engineer's IAM role has AdministratorAccess attached. An OU-level SCP explicitly denies cloudtrail:StopLogging for every account in that OU. What happens when the engineer tries to stop CloudTrail logging?
options: The action is denied, because an SCP's explicit deny overrides IAM-level permissions, even AdministratorAccess
The action succeeds, because AdministratorAccess always overrides any SCP
AWS prompts the engineer to choose which policy should win
The SCP is ignored because it was attached at the OU level instead of directly to the account
questions.explain: SCPs sit above IAM evaluation. An explicit Deny in an applicable SCP blocks the action regardless of how broad the principal's IAM permissions are, exactly like an explicit Deny inside IAM itself always wins.

questions.q: For an IAM principal's request to actually succeed, what has to be true?
options: Only the SCPs covering the account need to allow it; IAM policies are optional once Organizations is enabled
Only the identity-based IAM policy needs to allow it; SCPs are advisory only
Either IAM or the applicable SCPs need to allow it, whichever is more permissive
Both the IAM-level policies (identity-based, resource-based, boundaries) and every applicable SCP need to allow it — any one denial anywhere blocks the request
questions.explain: SCPs add another ceiling on top of ordinary IAM evaluation rather than replacing it. A request only succeeds when IAM and every applicable SCP both agree to allow it.
